Unit 1: Version Control and the DevOps Software Lifecycle
Completion status: [ ] Not started [ ] In progress [ ] Completed Date: __________
Learning objectives

Explain why version control exists.

Compare local, centralized and distributed version control.

Place Git inside a modern DevOps delivery pipeline. Why this matters in DevOps
DevOps depends on traceability. Infrastructure code, application code, configuration, deployment
manifests and operational documentation must all have controlled history. The problem before version control
Without version control, teams overwrite files, lose working versions, cannot prove who changed what,
and cannot reliably reproduce releases. File names such as final_v2_really_final are not a governance
system. Three version-control models

Local version control stores history on one machine.

Centralized version control uses one central server; clients check out working copies.

Distributed version control gives each clone a complete repository history, improving resilience and
offline work. Git in the delivery chain
A typical flow is: issue -> branch -> commits -> pull request -> automated checks -> review -> merge ->
build artifact -> deployment -> monitoring -> rollback if needed. How companies use this
Companies connect commits and pull requests to tickets, CI results, security scans, releases and
production incidents. This produces an auditable chain from requirement to running change. Common mistakes and prevention

Treating Git as only a backup tool.

Committing generated artifacts or secrets without policy.

Making production changes outside version control. Hands-on lab

Distinguish system, global and local configuration. Why this matters in DevOps
Correct configuration prevents inconsistent branch names, broken line endings and commits with incorrect

System settings affect all users. Global settings affect one user. Local settings affect one repository and
override broader scopes. Identity and behavior
Git records author and committer metadata. Teams also standardize default branch names, pull strategy,
editor and line-ending behavior. Command laboratory

Unit 3: Repositories, Working Tree, Index and Commit History
Completion status: [ ] Not started [ ] In progress [ ] Completed Date: __________
Learning objectives

Explain the three main local states.

Create a repository and inspect status.

Move changes through working tree, index and repository. Why this matters in DevOps
Most Git confusion comes from not understanding where a change currently lives. The three-state model
The working tree contains editable files. The index, also called staging area, is the proposed next
snapshot. The repository stores committed history. Snapshot thinking
Git commits are snapshots connected by parent relationships, not merely patches. Git can calculate
differences between snapshots when needed. Command laboratory
Create repository
mkdir git-state-lab
cd git-state-lab
git init
echo '# Git State Lab' > README.md
git status
The file is untracked until added. Stage and commit
git add README.md
git status
git commit -m "docs: add initial README"
git log --oneline --decorate
The commit records the staged snapshot. Compare states
echo 'Second line' >> README.md
git diff
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git diff compares working tree to index; --staged compares index to HEAD. How companies use this
Code reviews evaluate the staged and committed changes that become part of a pull request. CI systems
build from commits, not from a developer's uncommitted working tree.

Unit 4: Commit Design, Messages and Atomic Changes
Completion status: [ ] Not started [ ] In progress [ ] Completed Date: __________
Learning objectives

Create atomic commits.

Write professional commit messages.

Use commit metadata responsibly. Why this matters in DevOps
Small, coherent commits make reviews, reverts, debugging and release notes safer. Atomic commit principle
One commit should represent one logical change. A change may touch several files, but they should serve
the same purpose. Message structure
A useful message has a concise imperative subject, optional explanation of why, and references to issues
when appropriate. Conventional style
Many teams use prefixes such as feat, fix, docs, test, refactor, build, ci and chore. The exact convention is
less important than consistency. Command laboratory
Review before commit
git status
git diff
git diff --staged
Review content before creating history. Commit with body
git commit -m "fix: prevent empty deployment target" -m "Validate the environment before invoking the
release command."
The body explains motivation and important consequences. Amend safely
git commit --amend
Amend unpublished local commits. Avoid rewriting shared history without coordination. How companies use this
Organizations may validate commit formats, require signed commits, link commits to tickets, and
generate changelogs from structured messages. Common mistakes and prevention

Messages such as update or changes.

Mixing formatting, feature work and unrelated fixes.

Amending a shared commit and force-pushing without coordination.

Unit 5: Git Objects and Internal Architecture
Completion status: [ ] Not started [ ] In progress [ ] Completed Date: __________
Learning objectives

Identify blob, tree, commit and tag objects.

Understand content-addressable storage.

Inspect repository objects safely. Why this matters in DevOps
Git internals explain why identical content is reused, why commits are immutable and how history is
connected. Object types

A blob stores file content, not its filename.

A tree maps names to blobs and subtrees.

A commit references a root tree, parent commit or commits, author, committer and message.

An annotated tag object can point to another object and carry metadata and a signature. Content addressing
Objects are named by cryptographic hashes derived from their type, length and content. Changing the
content produces a different object identifier. References
Branches and tags are human-friendly references to object IDs. HEAD usually points symbolically to the
current branch. Command laboratory
Inspect object IDs
git rev-parse HEAD
git cat-file -t HEAD
git cat-file -p HEAD
cat-file reveals the type and content of an object. Inspect tree
git ls-tree HEAD
git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}
The tree connects path names to object IDs. Hash a file
git hash-object README.md
This computes the blob ID without changing the file. Common mistakes and prevention

Editing files inside .git manually.

Assuming a branch stores copies of every file.

Believing hashes are random identifiers. Hands-on lab

Unit 6: Branches, HEAD and Detached HEAD
Completion status: [ ] Not started [ ] In progress [ ] Completed Date: __________
Learning objectives

Create and switch branches.

Explain branch pointers.

Recover safely from detached HEAD. Why this matters in DevOps
Branches isolate streams of work and allow multiple changes to progress without overwriting one another. Branch model
A branch is a movable reference to a commit. Creating a commit advances the currently checked-out
branch. HEAD
HEAD identifies the current checkout. Normally it points to a branch. In detached HEAD state it points
directly to a commit. Branch naming
Professional teams use readable names tied to work, for example feature/login-rate-limit or fix/payment-
timeout. Command laboratory
Create branches
git switch -c feature/readme-details
echo 'Details' >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: expand README"
git branch -vv
switch -c creates and checks out a branch. Detached HEAD
git switch --detach HEAD~1
git status
git switch main
Detached checkout is useful for inspection, but new commits need a branch if they must be retained. Recover a detached commit
git switch -c recovery/important-work
Create a branch before leaving the detached commit. How companies use this
Teams map branches to pull requests, automated preview environments and policy checks. Long-lived
branches require careful synchronization and increase integration risk. Common mistakes and prevention

Creating work in detached HEAD and losing the reference.

Using vague branch names.

Learning objectives

Integration is where independent work becomes one tested history. Fast-forward merge
When the target branch has not diverged, its pointer can move directly to the source tip. Three-way merge
When both branches have new work, Git compares their tips and common ancestor and creates a merge
commit. Conflict resolution
A conflict means Git needs a human decision. Resolve meaning, not only markers. Then test the combined
behavior. Command laboratory
Merge a feature

git merge feature/readme-details
Inspect the output to identify fast-forward or merge commit behavior. Conflict workflow
git status
git diff
# edit conflicted files

git commit
git status is the primary guide during conflict resolution. Abort merge
git merge --abort
Abort when the integration must be restarted from a clean state. How companies use this
Protected branches usually require pull requests, automated checks and approvals before the server
performs or permits a merge. Common mistakes and prevention

Removing conflict markers without understanding both changes.

Merging with failing tests.

Resolving generated lockfiles casually without regeneration.

Unit 8: Rebase and History Rewriting
Completion status: [ ] Not started [ ] In progress [ ] Completed Date: __________
Learning objectives

Explain rebase accurately.

Rebase a private feature branch.

Use force-with-lease instead of unsafe force. Why this matters in DevOps
Rebase can simplify local history, but it replaces commits and therefore must be governed carefully. What rebase does
Rebase identifies commits unique to the current branch, resets the branch onto a new base, and replays
equivalent changes as new commits. Private versus shared history
Rewriting unpublished work is usually safe. Rewriting commits other people already use causes
divergence and recovery work. Interactive rebase
Interactive mode can reorder, squash, reword, edit or drop commits before publication. Command laboratory
Update a feature branch
git switch feature/readme-details
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
Resolve conflicts, add files and continue with git rebase --continue. Interactive cleanup
git rebase -i HEAD~3
Use only on commits that are safe to rewrite. Safer force push
git push --force-with-lease
This refuses to overwrite remote work you have not seen. How companies use this
Some teams prefer rebase-and-merge for a linear main branch; others preserve merge commits for
integration context. The policy should be explicit. Common mistakes and prevention

Rebasing a shared branch.

Using git push --force on protected or collaborative branches.

Squashing useful troubleshooting context into one enormous commit. Hands-on lab

Unit 9: Undoing Changes: Restore, Reset, Revert and Reflog
Completion status: [ ] Not started [ ] In progress [ ] Completed Date: __________
Learning objectives

Choose the correct undo tool.

Recover deleted or rewritten history.

Distinguish local history editing from shared-history reversal. Why this matters in DevOps
Production engineers must recover safely without destroying teammates' work. Restore
git restore changes working-tree or staged content depending on options. Reset
git reset moves a branch and optionally adjusts index and working tree. Soft, mixed and hard modes have
different effects. Revert
git revert creates a new commit that applies the inverse of an earlier commit. It is normally safest for
shared history. Reflog
Reflog records recent local reference movements and is a powerful recovery mechanism. Command laboratory
Discard unstaged change
git restore README.md
This is destructive for uncommitted content. Unstage while keeping work
git restore --staged README.md
The working-tree modification remains. Revert published commit
git revert <commit-id>
A new commit records the reversal. Recover with reflog
git reflog
git branch recovery <object-id>
Create a branch at the desired previous state before experimenting further. How companies use this
Incident responders often use revert to restore production quickly, then create a separate forward fix after
analysis. Common mistakes and prevention

Using reset --hard without checking uncommitted work.

Resetting a published branch and force-pushing.

Assuming reflog exists on every remote or forever. Hands-on lab

Learning objectives

Create lightweight and annotated tags.

Deployments need durable identifiers that connect source, artifacts, change records and rollback targets. Tags
A lightweight tag is a direct reference. An annotated tag is a first-class object with tagger, date, message
and optional signature. Semantic versioning
A common form is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: incompatible change, backward-compatible feature, backward-
compatible fix. Real policies may include pre-release identifiers. Release integrity
A release should point to an exact commit, and built artifacts should be traceable to that commit and
preferably immutable. Command laboratory
Create annotated tag
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release version 1.0.0"
git show v1.0.0
Annotated tags are preferred for formal releases. Push tags
git push origin v1.0.0
git push origin --tags
Push only intended tags in controlled workflows. Create source archive
git archive --format=tar.gz --output=release-v1.0.0.tar.gz v1.0.0
Archive exports tracked files from the tagged tree. How companies use this
Release pipelines can trigger from protected tags, build signed artifacts, publish checksums and update
deployment records. Common mistakes and prevention

Moving an already published release tag.

Tagging an untested commit.
